subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
description: Students define the appropriate quantities to measure when building a descriptive model of a real-world situation. Given a goal or question (for example, 'Which phone plan is the better deal?' or 'Is this stadium crowded?'), the student decides what to measure, chooses a sensible unit, identifies whether the quantity should be a count, a total, a rate, a ratio, a per-capita figure, or a percent, and judges whether a proposed quantity is relevant and well defined. This is a modeling and reasoning skill: there is often no single arithmetic answer, but there are clearly better and worse choices, and a good choice is operationally definable, measurable, and aligned with the question being asked.
subSkills: Translate a vague modeling goal into one or more measurable quantities
Choose an appropriate unit and scale for a quantity (for example dollars per month vs. dollars per year, people per square mile vs. total people)
Distinguish a count, a total, a rate, a ratio, a per-capita quantity, and a percent, and pick the right type for the question
Recognize when a per-unit or rate quantity (rather than a raw total) is needed for a fair comparison
Judge whether a proposed quantity is operationally well defined (can two people measure it and agree?)
Identify quantities that are irrelevant to or insufficient for answering the modeling question
Specify the level of precision and the range of values a quantity can reasonably take

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the quantity to measure
problemArchetypes.example: A school wants to know whether its cafeteria is too crowded at lunch. Name one quantity, with its unit, that best captures 'crowdedness,' and explain why it is better than simply counting the total number of students enrolled.

problemArchetypes.name: Pick the right unit or scale
problemArchetypes.example: A city manager is comparing water use across neighborhoods of very different sizes. Should water use be reported in total gallons per month or in gallons per person per day? Justify the choice for a fair comparison.

problemArchetypes.name: Rate or ratio vs. raw total for fair comparison
problemArchetypes.example: Country $A$ produces $1{,}200{,}000$ tons of wheat and Country $B$ produces $400{,}000$ tons. To decide which country is more agriculturally productive, what quantity should you define instead of comparing the totals, and what unit would it carry?

problemArchetypes.name: Judge whether a proposed quantity is well defined or relevant
problemArchetypes.example: To compare two streaming services, a student proposes the quantity 'number of good movies.' Explain why this quantity is not well defined for a model, and define a measurable quantity that could replace it.

problemArchetypes.name: Define quantities to model a multi-part decision
problemArchetypes.example: You are choosing between two cell phone plans. Plan $X$ costs $\$30$ per month plus $\$0.10$ per GB; Plan $Y$ costs $\$45$ per month with unlimited data. List the quantities (with units) you must define to model total yearly cost as a function of monthly data use $d$, measured in GB.

problemArchetypes.name: Specify precision and reasonable range
problemArchetypes.example: A model estimates the average speed of cars on a residential street to help set a speed limit. State an appropriate unit, a sensible level of precision (to the nearest what?), and a reasonable range of values the quantity could take.

difficultyRubric._split: tier1 = Easy to Medium (define and select quantities from a clearly framed prompt). tier2 = Medium to Hard (compare candidate quantities, justify units/precision, and define a system of quantities for a multi-step model). The single ramped worksheet runs Easy items 1 to 5, Medium 6 to 11, Hard 12 to 15.

Easy.description: The modeling goal is stated plainly and points to one obvious quantity. The student names the quantity and attaches a correct, conventional unit, or selects the best quantity/unit from a short list. One conceptual step; minimal justification.
constraints: Single quantity to define or choose
Unit is conventional and unambiguous (dollars, hours, miles per hour, people)
Multiple-choice or short-answer with a clearly best option
No comparison across differently sized groups required

Medium.description: The student must decide on the TYPE of quantity (total vs. rate vs. ratio vs. per-capita vs. percent) so the model is fair or meaningful, and justify the unit or scale. Often requires recognizing that a raw total is misleading and a per-unit quantity is needed.
constraints: Requires choosing among count / total / rate / ratio / per-capita / percent
Involves a fair comparison across groups of different size
Student must state the unit AND give a one-sentence justification
May ask to flag a proposed quantity as not well defined and fix it

Hard.description: The student defines a coherent SET of quantities (with units) needed to model a multi-part decision, specifies precision and reasonable ranges, and evaluates trade-offs between competing quantity choices. There is no single numeric answer; the response is judged on completeness, measurability, and alignment to the question.
constraints: Define two or more interrelated quantities for one model
Specify units, level of precision, and a reasonable range for at least one quantity
Justify why the chosen quantities answer the modeling question better than a named alternative
May tie quantities together (for example cost as a function of a defined variable with its unit)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student compares raw totals instead of defining a rate or per-capita quantity
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Option claims the better quantity is 'total amount' (for example total wheat in tons, total water in gallons) when the question demands a fair comparison across differently sized groups, so a per-unit or per-person quantity is required

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a quantity that is not operationally well defined
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Option proposes a vague, unmeasurable quantity such as 'number of good movies' or 'how fun the park is' that two observers could not measure and agree on

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses an inappropriate or inconsistent unit or scale
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Option attaches the wrong unit or scale (for example reporting a speed in 'miles' instead of 'miles per hour,' or population density in 'total people' instead of 'people per square mile')

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student selects a quantity that is irrelevant to the stated modeling goal
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Option names a real but off-target quantity (for example using 'total enrollment' to judge cafeteria crowding, or 'ticket price' to judge how fast a ride is) that does not bear on the question asked

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a percent or ratio with a count or total
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Option reports a quantity as a raw count when the question calls for a percent or ratio (for example '300 students passed' instead of 'percent of students who passed'), making comparison across groups invalid

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores precision or gives an unreasonable level of detail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Option states an absurd precision or range for the context (for example average car speed 'to the nearest thousandth of a mile per hour,' or a human height quantity allowing values like $40$ feet)

_comment_itemCounts: Single ramped worksheet (Easy->Hard across 15 items). tier1/tier2 are defined for completeness per the difficultyRubric._split but this standard uses the single sheet by default. Lesson 5+5, quiz 8 (all multiple choice with one clearly best, well-defined-quantity answer and distractors drawn from commonMisconceptions).
